children: Binance lost approximately $6.3 billion from its hot wallets in roughly 20 minutes on October 29, 2026. The rest of the crypto industry is now quietly checking its own locks.

Exchanges are reinforcing their defenses and pushing for faster sharing of threat information. The timing is uncomfortable. Crypto platforms are becoming more embedded in mainstream finance just as the biggest name in the business showed how quickly a vault can be emptied.
The attack began at approximately 20:05 UTC on October 29. Within about 20 minutes, attackers had drained around $6.3 billion in digital assets from the exchange's hot wallets.

Hot wallets are the internet-connected accounts exchanges use to process everyday withdrawals. Think of them as the cash drawer at the front of the store, not the safe in the back. They are convenient, and that convenience makes them a target.

Blockchain analytics firms TRM Labs, Chainalysis, and Elliptic have linked the theft with high confidence to TraderTraitor. That North Korean hacking group is associated with the Lazarus Group, a name that shows up in crypto breach reports with depressing regularity.
The damage could have been worse. Around $3 billion of the stolen assets, mostly the stablecoins USDT and USDC, was frozen on-chain by their issuers, Tether and Circle.

Stablecoin issuers can blacklist specific wallet addresses. Once flagged, the tokens in those addresses become effectively unspendable. In this case, that switch locked up close to half the haul before it could move far.

Binance has pledged to cover all user losses. The exchange is drawing on its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, along with corporate reserves. The combined commitment totals over $6.34 billion, including a $1 billion SAFU reserve.

The exchange temporarily paused withdrawals while it ran security reviews. Deposits stayed open, and Binance said it planned a swift resumption. It also told users that individual balances would not be directly affected.
So far, there is no reported evidence that private keys were leaked.
Kraken said it was watching industry incidents for lessons it could apply to its own defenses.

The loudest message from the sector is about speed. Exchanges are calling for faster sharing of threat intelligence, so that an attack pattern spotted at one platform can be flagged to others before it repeats.

The freeze of roughly $3 billion in stablecoins makes the case on its own. Coordinated, rapid action by Tether and Circle recovered more value than most exchange-level defenses ever could after the fact.
Before this month, the largest crypto theft on record was the roughly $1.5 billion taken from Bybit in February 2025. That attack was also tied to North Korean hackers.
The Binance breach is more than four times that size.

The scale also stands out against Binance's own safety net. The exchange's $1 billion SAFU reserve, once pitched as a backstop for exactly this kind of event, covers only a fraction of the loss. The company is leaning heavily on corporate reserves to make users whole.
Prices across major digital assets declined after the breach. The incident also sharpened skepticism about how centralized exchanges handle customer custody.
Binance's pledge to absorb the losses is expected to ease short-term panic. Users who see their balances intact are less likely to rush for the exits.

The stablecoin freeze showed that centrally issued tokens can be a powerful recovery tool when hackers grab them. It also reminded everyone that issuers hold a switch that can lock funds at the address level.

title: Crypto exchanges tighten security after $6.3 billion Binance hack
